# LiteParse

[![Crates.io version](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/liteparse.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/liteparse)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/Apache-2.0)

Rust library and CLI for fast, lightweight PDF and document parsing with spatial text extraction. Runs entirely locally with zero cloud dependencies.

> LiteParse is also available for [Node.js/TypeScript](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@llamaindex/liteparse), [Python](https://pypi.org/project/liteparse/), and the [browser (WASM)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@llamaindex/liteparse-wasm). See the [project README](https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse) for all options.

## Installation

Add to your `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
liteparse = "2"
```

Or install the CLI:

```bash
cargo install liteparse
```

## Quick Start

```rust
use liteparse::{LiteParse, LiteParseConfig};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let parser = LiteParse::new(LiteParseConfig::default());
    let result = parser.parse("document.pdf").await?;

    println!("{}", result.text);

    for page in &result.pages {
        println!("Page {}: {} text items", page.page_num, page.text_items.len());
    }

    Ok(())
}
```

## Configuration

```rust
use liteparse::{LiteParse, LiteParseConfig, OutputFormat};

let config = LiteParseConfig {
    ocr_enabled: true,                    // Enable OCR (default: true)
    ocr_language: "eng".to_string(),      // Tesseract language code
    ocr_server_url: None,                 // HTTP OCR server URL (optional)
    tessdata_path: None,                  // Path to tessdata directory (optional)
    max_pages: 1000,                      // Max pages to parse
    target_pages: Some("1-5,10".into()),  // Specific pages (optional)
    dpi: 150.0,                           // Rendering DPI
    output_format: OutputFormat::Json,    // Json | Text | Markdown
    extract_annotations: false,           // Include page annotations in output
    extract_structure_tree: false,        // Include tagged-PDF logical structure
    preserve_very_small_text: false,      // Keep tiny text
    extract_text_metadata: false,         // Opt in to rich PDF text metadata
    password: None,                       // Password for protected documents
    quiet: false,                         // Suppress progress output
    ..Default::default()
};

let parser = LiteParse::new(config);
```

Set `extract_annotations: true` to populate `ParsedPage::annotations` with
annotation subtype, contents, author/title, PDF date strings, viewport-space
rectangle and quadpoint rectangles, and external link URI. It is independent
of `extract_links`, which controls Markdown link rendering. The field is
`None` when extraction is disabled.

Set `extract_structure_tree: true` to populate `ParsedPage::structure_tree` with
the complete tagged-PDF hierarchy: all roots, element type/ID, actual and alternate
text, title, typed scalar attributes, MCIDs, recursive children, and referenced link
annotations. Disabled pages use `None`; enabled untagged pages have no roots.

## Markdown Output

LiteParse can render documents directly to Markdown, including headings, tables, lists,
images, and links reconstructed from the spatial layout. Set
`output_format: OutputFormat::Markdown`; the rendered Markdown is returned on
`result.text`. Two related knobs control Markdown rendering:

- `image_mode` (`ImageMode::Placeholder` default | `Off` | `Embed`) — how raster
  images are surfaced in the output.
- `extract_images` (default `false`) — return embedded image bytes and metadata
  without changing Markdown image handling. This is the only option that enables
  extraction.
- `image_output_dir` — write extracted image files and return their names/paths;
  requires `extract_images: true`. Duplicate image resources reuse the same file.
- `extract_links` (default `true`) — render hyperlink annotations as
  `[text](url)`; set `false` for plain anchor text.

```rust
use liteparse::config::{ImageMode, LiteParseConfig, OutputFormat};

let config = LiteParseConfig {
    output_format: OutputFormat::Markdown,
    image_mode: ImageMode::Placeholder,
    extract_images: true,
    image_output_dir: Some("./images".into()),
    extract_links: true,
    ..Default::default()
};
let result = LiteParse::new(config).parse("document.pdf").await?;
println!("{}", result.text); // rendered Markdown
```

> Reconstruction quality varies with document complexity.

## Parsing from Bytes

```rust
use liteparse::types::PdfInput;

let pdf_bytes: Vec<u8> = std::fs::read("document.pdf")?;
let result = parser.parse_input(PdfInput::Bytes(pdf_bytes)).await?;
println!("{}", result.text);
```

## Document Complexity

Before committing to a full parse, check whether a document needs OCR or heavier
processing. `is_complex` is a cheap, text-layer-only pass that returns a
`PageComplexityStats` per page with a `needs_ocr` verdict and the signals behind it —
useful for routing documents to different pipelines, rejecting ones you can't handle, or
estimating cost.

```rust
use liteparse::types::PdfInput;

let parser = LiteParse::new(LiteParseConfig::default());
let pages = parser.is_complex(PdfInput::Path("document.pdf".into())).await?;

if pages.iter().any(|p| p.needs_ocr) {
    // Route to the OCR-enabled pipeline, inspect `p.reasons`, etc.
    for page in pages.iter().filter(|p| p.needs_ocr) {
        println!("Page {} needs OCR: {:?}", page.page_number, page.reasons);
    }
}
```

`reasons` is a `Vec<ComplexityReason>` (`Scanned`, `NoText`, `SparseText`,
`EmbeddedImages`, `Garbled`, `VectorText`, `AnnotationText`); new variants may be added over time, so match
leniently.

## Custom OCR Engine

Implement the `OcrEngine` trait to plug in your own OCR backend:

```rust
use liteparse::ocr::OcrEngine;
use std::sync::Arc;

let parser = LiteParse::new(LiteParseConfig::default())
    .with_ocr_engine(Arc::new(my_engine));
```

For a native ONNX backend, enable `oar-ocr` and supply a detection model,
recognition model, and matching character dictionary:

```rust,no_run
use liteparse::ocr::oar::OarOcrEngine;
use liteparse::{LiteParse, LiteParseConfig};
use std::path::Path;
use std::sync::Arc;

let models = Path::new("models");
let engine = OarOcrEngine::from_models(
    models.join("pp-ocrv6_small_det.onnx"),
    models.join("pp-ocrv6_small_rec.onnx"),
    models.join("ppocrv6_dict.txt"),
)?;

let parser = LiteParse::new(LiteParseConfig::default())
    .with_ocr_engine(Arc::new(engine));
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

For opt-in model downloads, enable `oar-ocr-auto-download` and use a preset. On
first use, `oar-ocr` downloads the detection model, recognition model, and
matching dictionary from ModelScope, verifies their SHA-256 digests, and caches
them under `$OAR_HOME` (default `~/.oar`):

```rust,no_run
use liteparse::ocr::oar::OarOcrEngine;

// Smallest / fastest PP-OCRv6 configuration.
let engine = OarOcrEngine::ppocr_v6_tiny()?;
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

Presets cover the current and previous PP-OCR generations, from fastest to most
accurate: `ppocr_v6_tiny`, `ppocr_v6_small`, and `ppocr_v6_medium`. Each wires the correct
detector/recognizer/dictionary trio. For PP-OCRv4, a language-specific
recognizer, or a custom mix, use `from_models` with a matching dictionary.

To mix a detector, recognizer, and dictionary yourself, pass registered bare
file names to `from_models`. Pair the recognizer with its matching dictionary —
the tiny recognizer needs `ppocrv6_tiny_dict.txt`, while the larger models use
`ppocrv6_dict.txt`; a mismatched dictionary silently produces garbled text:

```rust,no_run
use liteparse::ocr::oar::OarOcrEngine;

let engine = OarOcrEngine::from_models(
    "pp-ocrv6_small_det.onnx",
    "pp-ocrv6_small_rec.onnx",
    "ppocrv6_dict.txt",
)?;
# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())
```

All three artifacts also accept in-memory bytes, so the whole pipeline can be
embedded with `include_bytes!` rather than shipped as files. Use `OAROCRBuilder`
with `OarOcrEngine::from_builder` for model-specific settings or optional
orientation and rectification models. The fallible constructors return
`liteparse::LiteParseError`. All constructors use conservative batch sizes and
serialize page inference to avoid multiplying inference memory across
concurrently scheduled pages.
`OcrOptions::language` is not interpreted: the recognition model and character
dictionary define the supported languages, and a configured `ocr_language`
triggers a one-time warning to make that explicit.

## Features

- **`tesseract`** (default) — Built-in Tesseract OCR via `tesseract-rs`. Disable with `default-features = false` if you don't need OCR or want to use an HTTP OCR server instead.
- **`oar-ocr`** — Optional native ONNX backend via `oar-ocr`. Local or in-memory models; non-WASM Rust API only.
- **`oar-ocr-auto-download`** — Enables SHA-256-verified download and caching of registered model file names through `oar-ocr`.
- **`oar-ocr-cuda`**, **`oar-ocr-tensorrt`**, **`oar-ocr-directml`**, **`oar-ocr-coreml`**, **`oar-ocr-webgpu`**, **`oar-ocr-openvino`** — Forward the selected ONNX Runtime execution provider to `oar-ocr`.

The Node.js, Python, and WASM bindings build LiteParse with default features
disabled and do not expose these OAR features, so their published binaries do
not inherit the OAR model or runtime dependency footprint.

## Supported Formats

- PDF (`.pdf`)
- Microsoft Office (`.docx`, `.xlsx`, `.pptx`, etc.) — requires LibreOffice
- OpenDocument (`.odt`, `.ods`, `.odp`) — requires LibreOffice
- Images (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.tiff`, etc.)

## CLI

The crate also builds the `lit` CLI binary:

```bash
lit parse document.pdf
lit parse document.pdf --format json -o output.json
lit parse document.pdf --format markdown -o output.md
lit screenshot document.pdf -o ./screenshots
lit batch-parse ./input ./output
lit is-complex document.pdf
```

See `lit --help` for all options.

# rune-motion

Rune's animation runtime: springs, tweens, decay, keyframes, retargeting, presence and
transitions (blur-replace included), layout animation, matched geometry and choreography. It is
plain math and data structures with no renderer dependency and no required dependencies (the
optional `serde` feature covers the config types). App code states targets. The render thread
samples them once per frame and gets back what to draw.

```rust
use rune_motion::prelude::*;

let mut scene = Scene::new();
let card = NodeId(1);

// The first build never animates.
scene.insert(card, NodeSpec::new(Rect::new(0.0, 0.0, 320.0, 80.0)).radius(12.0), Mount::Initial);

// Later: a new row blurs in place, the card reflows with width leading, then something leaves.
let row = NodeId(2);
scene.insert(row, NodeSpec::new(Rect::new(0.0, 96.0, 320.0, 44.0))
    .parent(card)
    .transition(Transition::blur_replace()), Mount::Animated);
scene.set_frame(card, Rect::new(0.0, 0.0, 360.0, 160.0), LayoutAnim::new(motion::MORPH).width_leads());
scene.remove(NodeId(3));                       // stays drawn until its exit settles

let out = scene.frame_at(1.0 / 120.0);         // render thread, once per frame
for p in out.changed { /* draw p.rect, p.opacity, p.affine(), p.blur, p.mask … */ }
```

Without a scene graph, the store animates any property directly:

```rust
let mut store = AnimationStore::new();
store.set(id, prop::OPACITY, 0.0);
store.animate(id, prop::OPACITY, 1.0, motion::SETTLE);            // spring, bounce 0
store.animate(id, prop::FRAME, rect, motion::MORPH.delay(0.05));  // edges, delayed
store.animate(id, X, 40.0, Curve::ease_in_out(0.3).completion(7)); // tween, Completed{token: 7}
store.release(id, X, fling_v, Release::DecayClamped { decay: Decay::IOS_NORMAL, min: 0.0, max, spring: motion::SNAP });
store.tick_at(now);
let x = store.get(id, X);
```

### Kit's motion rules are the defaults

- Springs are duration plus bounce, with bounce 0 by default. Exits run 10–25 % shorter than entrances.
- Interrupting a motion keeps its position and velocity.
- Nothing animates on first mount. A track's first `animate` acts as `set`, and setting an unchanged target does nothing.
- The user's direct manipulation is never animated. Gestures write values with `set` and animate only on `release`.
- Under reduced motion, travel, scale, shape and blur change instantly, and opacity, colour and presence take a 0.18 s ease-in-out fade (`REDUCED_FADE`). Gesture values keep their curve. `match_geometry` turns into a crossfade in place.
- Both edges of a rect snap to 1/64 device px, and settle thresholds scale with the pixel density.
- Blur is limited to 4 px and only applies to things entering or leaving in place. A transition that travels drops its blur. Scale stays within [0.9, 1.1] and never goes to 0; `Transition::allow_small_scale()` lowers the floor to 0.5 for small glyphs. A removed node always fades out (`Effect::kit_rules`).
- Width leads: `.width_leads()` runs the X spring at 0.78× the duration (taken from a launcher app).
- A stationary edge gets no motion at all.
- A node given `Scene::set_ride_trailing` keeps its place against its parent's trailing edge while the parent's width animates; its frame is still given in parent space.

## Design

**Analytic tracks.** Each value lane is `target + Σ offset layers`. A layer is a closed-form
segment: an underdamped, critical or overdamped spring, a decay, a tween or a Hermite cubic. Each
one is evaluated directly at the frame's timestamp. Nothing is integrated step by step, so
results are the same at any frame rate. Sampling at the display link's *target* timestamp is
exact, frames can be skipped, and tests can jump to any `t`. Each layer stores its own settle
time, an upper bound that holds for the whole tail (spring envelopes, or bisection for the
critical and overdamped cases). Once that time passes, the track snaps to `(target, 0)`, leaves
the active list and costs nothing.

**Merge vs additive.** Springs, decay and keyframes *merge* by default: the store samples
`(x, v)` and starts one new segment from there, like SwiftUI spring merging or Compose
`animateTo`. That keeps one layer per lane and O(1) sampling. Tweens *add* by default, Core
Animation style: the running curves continue, and a new layer animates the target delta to 0, so
every curve keeps its shape. A test checks that additive springs give exactly the same result as
merged springs. A lane holds at most 8 additive layers. Past that, they collapse into one merged
segment.

**Struct of arrays.** Track data lives in flat lane arrays (layer, target, value, velocity), with
generational `TrackId`s, a dense `active` list, free-list pools for extra layers and delayed
starts, and an Fx-style hash map from `(node, prop)` to track. A tick walks only the active
tracks, reads contiguous memory and does not allocate. `tests/alloc.rs` checks this with a
counting allocator.

**Deterministic math.** `math::exp` and `math::sin_cos` are custom polynomial versions (Estrin's
scheme, FMA on aarch64 or `+fma`, branchless quadrant fix-up). They don't depend on the
platform's libm, so traces and goldens stay stable, and they're cheap: 5 ns for `exp` and 7.6 ns
for `sin_cos`.

**Presence.** One `PRESENCE` progress (0 means absent, 1 means present) drives the insertion and
removal effects. If a node is reversed mid-flight (it comes back while exiting, or leaves while
entering), the effect endpoints are re-solved at the current visual state so nothing jumps.
`Travel::Screen` interpolates root-space start and end edges with a separate progress per axis.
`match_geometry` starts the target node at the source's exact presented rect, velocity, radius
and fill, then removes the source immediately.

## Renderer integration contract

Run this on the render thread once per display-link callback:

1. `scene.set_time(target_timestamp)`. Use the timestamp the frame will be *shown* at, not the
   current time. `Clock::frame(host)` handles pause, slow motion and seek.
2. Apply the commits that arrived since the last frame: `insert(id, spec, mount)`, `remove(id)`,
   `set_frame(id, rect, anim)`, `animate(id, prop, target, anim)`, `set(...)` and
   `match_geometry(from, to, anim)`. Pass `Mount::Initial` for the first build.
3. `let out = scene.frame()`, which returns a `FrameOutput`:
   - `changed: &[Presented]`: only the nodes whose presented values changed, parents before
     children.
   - `exited: &[NodeId]`: nodes whose exit settled. Stop drawing them and free their resources.
   - `events: &[MotionEvent]`: `Settled` and `Completed { token, finished }`, for app callbacks.
   - `animating: bool`: when false, pause the display link until the next commit.

`Presented` holds everything needed to draw one node:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rect` | Root-space rect. It already includes every ancestor's translation and this node's own, and both edges are snapped to 1/64 device px. Draw shapes, borders and shadows at this size. |
| `opacity` | This node's own opacity (presence × property). Apply ancestors' opacity as group opacity. |
| `transform`, `anchor` | Scale and rotation about the root-space `anchor`, composed down the tree like `CALayer`. `affine()` returns the 2×3 matrix. |
| `blur` | Own plus presence Gaussian sigma in points. 0 means attach no filter. Presence effects clamp to ≤ 4 pt; `blur_replace` peaks at 1.5 pt. Explicit property blur can remain at rest. |
| `radius`, `fill` | Animated corner radii, and the fill as sRGB with straight alpha (interpolated in premultiplied OKLab). |
| `mask` | `Mask { inset: Sides, feather: Sides }` in the node's own coordinates: how far each side is pulled in, and the gradient width on that side. Evaluate it as an SDF ramp. `mask.is_none()` means no clip. |
| `phase` | `Entering`, `Present` or `Exiting { generation }`. |
| `in_flow` | Turns false as soon as a popLayout exit starts. App layout should stop reserving space for the node. |
| `flags` | motion-trace bits (`flags::ANIMATED`, `ANCESTOR_ANIMATED`, `CLIPPED`, `FILTERED`) and intent bits (own `<< 8`, ancestor `<< 16`). |

Call `scene.set_pixel_scale(scale)` on display changes and `scene.set_reduced_motion(on)` when the
system setting changes. Setting `RUNE_MOTION_TRACE=/path.jsonl` and calling
`scene.set_trace(MotionTrace::from_env(&header))` writes motion traces.

- `Travel::Screen` uses a separate progress per axis, so a width-leading screen path is not perfectly straight.

# Global shortcuts

```rust,ignore
let app = App::new(spec)
    .global_shortcut("cmd+shift+space", |state, tx| {
        state.quick_panel_open = true;
        if let Some(token) = tx.activation_token() {
            state.app_handle.activate(token);
        } else {
            state.app_handle.open();
        }
    })
    .windowless();
app.run();
```

The handler receives the same state as its `App`/`WindowSpec`, on the app thread.
It runs through `Runtime::update`, including animation and shell requests. Native
activation wakes the loop even while no window is visible.

Static builder failures print once and can be drained with
`handle.take_shortcut_errors()`. The builder defers registration until the app's
host exists, so `run_windows_with` factories can construct apps normally.

Runtime registration returns the actual result:

```rust,ignore
let id = handle.register_shortcut("ctrl+alt+k".parse()?, |state, tx| {
    state.open_quick_panel(tx.activation_token());
})?;
handle.unregister_shortcut(id)?;
```

After a `Conflict`, `handle.shortcut_owner(&shortcut)` names the holder when Rune or
the desktop knows it: this App or another Rune App in the process (its `AppSpec`
title), or a macOS system shortcut ("Spotlight", "Mission Control", "Input Sources",
"Screenshot", "App Switcher", "macOS" for other enabled symbolic hotkeys), at the chord
the user remapped it to. The macOS lookup answers only on the main thread. A chord
another Rune App in the process holds is refused with `Conflict` on every backend. Other apps'
grabs, Windows, X11 and the portal name nobody, so it returns None. Headless runs
answer only for their own virtual registrations. `ShortcutError::Conflict` itself is
unchanged.

A chord needs ⌘, ⌃ or ⌥ (Ctrl, Alt or Super elsewhere), or an F1–F24 key, because a
global Space or ⇧A would take that key from typing in every app. Both the builder and
`register_shortcut` refuse one without them with `InvalidAccelerator`
(`shortcut.require_modifier()` checks it), unless the App opts in with
`.allow_unmodified_shortcuts()`.

Call runtime registration after the host starts (an `on_window` or queued
`handle.update` callback works, including one on another window of the same
`run_windows`). Calls before startup or after shutdown return `NotRunning`. On macOS/Windows other threads may call it, but wait for the app
thread, so the app thread must not join those callers. Linux registration can
run off-thread. Dropping the host unregisters everything,
even if other threads retain `AppHandle`s.

## Desktop behavior

- macOS: Carbon `RegisterEventHotKey`, no Accessibility permission. Command is
  the Super modifier. Hardware key positions follow the US layout; F21–F24 have
  no Carbon key code and return `InvalidAccelerator`.
- Windows: `RegisterHotKey` on a message-only window owned by the event thread.
  Repeat is disabled. Windows-reserved combinations may fail registration.
- X11: checked passive grabs on every root, including CapsLock/NumLock variants.
  A failed variant rolls back the registration. Autorepeat is filtered, so a held
  chord fires once, as on macOS and Windows. Keys use the current keymap's
  base keysyms; restart/re-register after changing the keymap.
- Wayland: xdg-desktop-portal GlobalShortcuts. No portal returns `Unsupported`.
  The portal may ask for permission or let the user choose another trigger;
  `preferred_trigger` is a preference, not an exclusive-grab guarantee. Cancellation
  is `PermissionDenied`, not `Conflict`. Each shortcut owns a portal session so
  unregister also works with version 1. The activation token is available only
  during its handler, through `Tx::activation_token()`.

Registration is synchronous, including portal consent, with a two-minute bound.
Register startup shortcuts before showing windows; use a worker thread for
runtime Wayland binding so a consent dialog does not block the event thread.

Only an actual registration creates native resources: macOS/Windows need no
listener thread; X11/Wayland each create a listener that is joined on teardown.
No-shortcut apps never open a shortcut display or portal connection.

Display normalizes modifiers to `ctrl+alt+shift+super`, then the lowercase key.
`cmd`, `command`, `meta`, and `logo` alias `super`; `option` aliases `alt`.

## Shortcut recorder

`rune_kit::ShortcutRecorder` uses app-owned `ShortcutRecorderState` and renders the
existing `Keybind` component:

```rust,ignore
ShortcutRecorder::new("shortcut", &state.shortcut, |s: &mut State| &mut s.shortcut)
    .on_change(|state, shortcut, tx| state.replace_shortcut(shortcut, tx))
    .build(&kit)
```

The change callback returns `Result<(), ShortcutError>`. A registration failure
retains the old binding; the recorder keeps showing the refused chord with a message
until another modifier starts the next chord. Unchanged chords skip the callback,
unless `state.mark_unregistered()` says the shortcut isn't registered (it failed at
launch): then recording it again retries it through the callback. The
default message names the chord ("⌃J is already in use."); `.error_message(|error,
chord| ...)` rewords it, falling back on `rune_kit::shortcut_error_message`, and
`ShortcutRecorderState::refused()` reads the chord. A chord without a modifier (other
than F1–F24) is refused before the callback with "Add ⌘, ⌃ or ⌥." unless
`.allow_unmodified()`.
Click or keyboard activation starts recording, held modifiers preview immediately,
Escape cancels, Backspace clears, and focus loss or disabling cancels recording.
Repeated key presses are consumed without registering again.
`scripts/shortcut-recorder.json` records a chord headlessly.

`Shortcut` stores a `PhysicalKeyCode`. Parsing and Display use canonical US physical
names; `keycaps()` is for display only. On the macOS main thread, printable labels
use `TISCopyCurrentKeyboardLayoutInputSource` and `UCKeyTranslate` without changing
the input source. Other platforms, background callers and unavailable layouts use
US labels. Persist the canonical shortcut, not its translated keycaps.
`menu_keycaps()` is the label a menu shows: the key the accelerator names on every
layout (`cmd+b` is ⌘B on Dvorak, where `keycaps()` says ⌘X). Use it for menu items and
hints of keys an app matches by character, `keycaps()` for global shortcuts.

Physical input and its logical fallback are processed together in event order.
Focused capture runs before modal Escape, text editing and paste. A consumed chord
never reads the clipboard. Otherwise eligible Cmd-V requests the asynchronous
clipboard worker and consumes the command even for empty/image-only clipboards.
The captured paste target prevents a later focus change from receiving the reply.
Single-line and secure editors retain their ordinary editing and copy protections.
Key-taking launcher panels retain winit's input view/delegate and use the window
input path; overlays and Wayland layer surfaces also forward physical input.

## Native application and Dock menus

```rust,ignore
let app = App::new(spec)
    .menu_item(MenuItem::new("Open Quick Panel", open_panel).id("quick")
        .key_equivalent("cmd+shift+space".parse()?))
    .menu_item(MenuItem::new("Preferences", preferences).menu("Tools"))
    .menu_item(MenuItem::new("Open Quick Panel", open_panel).id("dock-quick").dock())
    .menu_item(MenuItem::new("New Window", new_window).menu("File"))
    .menu_item(MenuItem::separator().menu("File"))
    .menu_item(MenuItem::new("Close Tab", close_tab).menu("File"));

handle.set_menu([
    MenuItem::new("Open Quick Panel", open_panel).id("quick")
        .enabled(true).checked(true),
])?;
```

Actions are `fn(&mut S, &mut Tx)` queued on the app thread. `set_menu` replaces all
custom items for that App; an empty list removes them. It validates atomically and
queues installation. `take_menu_errors()` reports deferred startup/installation
errors. Replaced, disabled or removed items invalidate stale queued actions.
`MenuItem::separator()` is a separator line (`NSMenuItem.separatorItem` on macOS), placed
with `menu` or `dock` in list order like any item. It needs no id, takes no part in
id/title lookup and can't be fired.

On macOS, one App owns the process-wide custom menus. Default Quit/Hide items and
existing named-menu items are preserved. The Dock adapter adds an absent
`applicationDockMenu:` selector to winit's existing delegate class, retaining the
delegate and all existing methods. An existing non-Rune selector is an error; the
Rune hook returns nil after teardown. Key equivalents are native menu equivalents,
not global registrations. AppKit matches them by the character typed, so an item's
equivalent is the character its accelerator names: `cmd+b` is "b" with ⌘ on every
layout, `cmd+shift+=` is "=" with ⇧⌘, and named keys use AppKit's characters (↩ ⇥ ⎋ ⌫ ⌦,
arrows, F-keys). App menu, named menus, Dock and context menus all show the same key.
When two items in the menu bar share an equivalent, AppKit gives it to the first and
the later one shows none, so one key never runs two items. Rune never sets the
function-key flag; the 🌐F in a menu titled View is AppKit's own Enter Full Screen.

An accessory app that calls `set_dock_icon(true)` gets winit's standard app menu
if `NSApp.mainMenu` is absent: About, Services, Hide, Hide Others, Show All and Quit.
Creating custom menu items first uses that same default root; adding them later
inserts alongside the defaults. Existing roots are never replaced, and clearing
custom items or calling `set_dock_icon(false)` leaves the default menu intact.
A regular app whose menu bar is still winit's default also gets the standard items
below; an accessory app gets them only with `standard_menus()`.

### Standard menus

`App::standard_menus()` adds an Edit menu (Undo ⌘Z, Redo ⇧⌘Z, Cut ⌘X, Copy ⌘C, Paste
⌘V, Select All ⌘A) and a Window menu (Minimize ⌘M, Close ⌘W) to the process menu bar
when the first window of that App starts. A regular (non-accessory) app gets the same
items without asking, as long as its menu bar is still winit's default when its first
window starts; an app that set its own menu bar is left alone. Rune never adds Quit:
an accessory app that later shows its Dock icon gets winit's app menu (with Quit) as
before. Items go into existing menus of the same title, an item whose action is
already there is skipped, and custom `MenuItem`s keep working in either order. A
custom item with a standard item's equivalent (Close Tab ⌘W) takes it: the standard
item shows none until the custom one goes, whichever was set first. New custom menus
take the Mac order: File before Edit, the app's other menus before Window, Help last.
Clearing custom items keeps a menu the standard items share. An accessory app's menu
bar is hidden, but AppKit still matches its key equivalents.

Every item has a nil target, so AppKit sends it to the key window's first responder:

- An AppKit window in the process (an open panel, an updater's window) gets the
  normal `copy:`, `paste:`, `selectAll:`, `undo:`, `performMiniaturize:` and
  `performClose:` of its focused field or window.
- A Rune window's first responder is winit's view. AppKit consumes a matched key
  equivalent even when no responder implements its action, which is why a plain Edit
  menu would swallow ⌘C before Rune sees it. So the view gains the eight actions (added
  to winit's view class, never replacing a method it has), and each hands Rune the key:
  the very event that fired the item, so text fields, `on_key` and shortcuts see exactly
  the `Key::Command` they did without the menu, once. A click on the item sends a
  made-up press and release of its key instead.
- An IME composition (or a dead key's accent) in the focused field ends first, as in an
  NSTextView: the input method commits it into the field, then the command acts. One
  that doesn't commit is dropped, so the key still reaches Rune.
- ⌘W and ⌘M reach Rune the same way first. If no handler takes them and the window has
  that title-bar button, the window then closes or minimizes as a click on the button
  would: `on_close` and `keep_running` hiding apply. A window without the button
  (borderless, an overlay or nonactivating panel) only gets the key. An app that binds ⌘W itself keeps it.

Without `standard_menus`, an accessory app's keys don't change.

Native Windows/Linux return `MenuError::Unsupported`; startup builders report it
through `take_menu_errors()`. Headless virtual menus work on every platform:
`{"menu":"Open Quick Panel"}` invokes by exact id or unambiguous title. Unknown,
disabled and ambiguous items fail the script.

`scripts/check-native-menu-macos.py <menu_probe>` exercises the app-menu click,
key equivalent, named-menu click, runtime enabled/checked updates, preservation of
Quit/Hide and the Dock delegate selector on a GUI test Mac, under the same lock.
`scripts/check-dock-menu-macos.py <dock_menu_probe>` checks the accessory-to-Regular
default menu in both orders. `scripts/menu.json` exercises title/id dispatch headlessly.

Start from a clean worktree. Keep unrelated edits in their own worktree.

```sh
git fetch origin
gh stack init --base main stack/example-core
```

Adopt existing branches with `gh stack init --base main existing/bottom existing/top`. Link existing PRs in dependency order with `gh stack link <bottom-pr> <top-pr>`, then manage their branches with `gh stack`. Keep unrelated changes in separate stacks.

## Where content goes

Each route sends content only to the destination listed for it.

| Route | Destination |
| --- | --- |
| Chrome built-in AI and the bundled local models | Your computer |
| Local model servers | The server on your computer: Ollama at 127.0.0.1:11434, LM Studio at 127.0.0.1:1234, llama.cpp at 127.0.0.1:8080, or the local address you set. Ollama can also offer cloud models, so check the model you select. |
| Your own API key in the extension | The service the key belongs to: OpenAI (api.openai.com), Anthropic (api.anthropic.com), Google (generativelanguage.googleapis.com), OpenRouter (openrouter.ai), or the OpenAI compatible endpoint you set. It receives your question, the page content you ask about and the conversation so far. |

| Installed agents (Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Pi) | The agent on your computer, which sends what it needs to the account and model you configured for it |
| Reading a page | When the page you ask about links to its own markdown copy on the same site over https, the extension fetches that copy from the site, without cookies, instead of reading the page's layout. No address on your computer or local network is fetched. |
| Dictionary lookups | The selected word goes to api.dictionaryapi.dev. Dictionary data files come from media.githubusercontent.com. |
| Search and language models | Once, on first use, the extension downloads its search model (8 MB, WhiteHades/blink-8M-int8) and its language detector (5 MB, WhiteHades/py3langid-compact) from huggingface.co, each at a fixed revision checked by its SHA-256. Nothing about you or your pages is sent; searches and detection run on your device. |

Installed agents' tools and metldr's browser tools can provide additional access, subject to the agent's permissions and metldr's browser approvals. Your provider's and agent's policies apply to their processing. Downloads you start contact the services that supply the requested files.

## What stays saved

The extension saves settings, cached summaries and page context in your browser. The companion saves conversations, results and recovery records on your computer. Installed agents can keep their own sessions and files.

The extension also saves usage records in your browser, including page addresses, domains, session activity, model use and feature events. Automatic deletion after a set period is not currently enabled. Remove the extension's browser data to delete those records.

API keys you add in the extension are encrypted with a key that cannot leave this browser profile, and only the encrypted form is saved, locally and never synced. Keys you add in the companion stay in its credential store, outside page scripts. Installed agents keep their own authentication.

Clearing the extension's cache or browser data does not remove companion records or agent files. Remove those separately using their storage locations and tools. The companion keeps its data in `~/.local/share/metldr`, or in `$XDG_DATA_HOME/metldr` when that is set.

## Browser access

Page permissions let metldr add its controls and read content for its features. The browser agent asks for approval before supported page changes. Installed agents also have their own permission rules.

Review your selected connection and permissions before sharing private content. For questions, use the support contact on the [Chrome Web Store listing](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/kbfdmfgmmibkdnbfdaeganjckfgbfjlh).

# Browse

Source: https://github.com/anomalyco/browse, Rust workspace under `rust/`, commit 6128d7b, MIT (LICENSE).

Vendored: `crates/browse-core` and `crates/browse-page` (sources and the page scripts in `js/`).
Each other Browse crate comes in with the change that first uses it.

Changes from upstream:
- `browse-page/src/page.rs`: Browse's isolated world is created without universal access, which
  the metldr extension refuses.
- `browse-page/src/scripts.rs` and `lib.rs`: `injected_source()` and `helpers()` are public, so the
  metldr extension can ship both scripts as files and the companion sends a short marker instead.
- `Cargo.toml`: tokio builds only the features the two crates use (rt, sync, time, macros, fs)
  instead of `full`.
- Left out: the Chromium integration tests and the `js/generate.sh` script that rebuilds the page
  scripts from Playwright.

# LiteParse

Source: https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse, `crates/liteparse` at commit a684a4a (2.20.0), Apache-2.0 (LICENSE).

Vendored: `crates/liteparse` (sources). PDFium and its Rust bindings come from crates.io
(`liteparse-pdfium` and `liteparse-pdfium-sys` 1.14.0); the PDFium library itself is the
`chromium/8058` wasm build, fetched by `scripts/build-rust.mjs` and used only when its SHA-256
matches the pinned value.

Changes from upstream:
- `markdown_layout/repetition.rs`: single-page header and footer detection matches each line
  against the chrome patterns once, not once per pair of lines (the pass was quadratic).
- `projection.rs`: font-name hints are found in one pass over the name instead of a substring
  search per hint for every text item.
- `markdown_layout/paragraphs.rs`: whitespace collapses by copying whole words.
- `conversion.rs`: the browser build reads PDFs only and refuses other inputs, so the image and
  office converters stay out of the module.
- `Cargo.toml`: a standalone crate; PDFium from crates.io pinned to 1.14.0.
- Left out: the `lit` command line tool, the Tesseract and OAR OCR backends, the tests,
  examples and benchmarks.

Each change keeps the markdown output byte-identical on the upstream test PDFs and the four
reference papers used to measure it.

# py3langid

Source: https://github.com/markusmobius/rust-py3langid, crate `rust-py3langid` 0.4.1, BSD-3-Clause
(LICENSE), itself a port of py3langid (langid.py by Marco Lui and Timothy Baldwin).

Changes from upstream:
- `model.rs`: the model in compact form: int8 weights with one scale per feature, and the byte
  automaton as each row's differences from the start row (a 256-bit mask and its targets, found
  by population count). About 25 MB in memory instead of 97 MB; on the papluca
  language-identification test set the answers match upstream's (99.14% on sentences, 93.62%
  against 93.65% on four-word spans).
- `original.rs`: the upstream LIDG2 reader, kept only to convert a model (feature `pack`, binary
  `pack-langid`).
- `preprocess.rs`: case tests and lowercasing through the standard library instead of ICU (the
  same Unicode data, about 100 KB less wasm).
- `identifier.rs`: transitions through `Model::next`, scores from int8 weights; the embedded model
  and file helpers removed (the extension downloads the packed model).
- Left out: the embedded model file, upstream tests, benchmarks and examples.

# Rune source

Source: https://github.com/anomalyco/rune
Revision: 781e2b6d87cd5f32d6f4365956fad4baaf24ee50

This directory keeps the Rune runtime, motion, staging, layout and optional profiling crates with their original relative paths. The workspace lists these crates and retains the upstream edition, license and lint settings. Dependency versions are owned by the consuming crate lockfile.

Local changes:

* The browser calls the existing frame-drawn hook after presentation, allowing restricted answer frames to follow submitted canvas geometry.
* Application fallback fonts are registered for Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari, Bengali and Thai as well as CJK. Browser symbol fallback recognizes the supplied Noto Sans Symbols 2 family.
* The WebAssembly GPU instance cache uses thread local storage; native targets retain the upstream mutex.
* Browser field semantics share Rust paths and focus state with the existing text service bridge. Secure field values are omitted from the semantic mirror.
* Disabled fields cannot take focus through traversal or restoration, or retain offscreen editing focus.
* Text test fixtures use the identical font already bundled in the runtime.
* Focus and semantic mirror regressions cover these changes.
* A composition whose end event is refused as untrusted is finished by the next trusted input or key that is no longer composing, so the field never stays in a preedit. Mirror nodes rewrite their style only when it changes.
* `El::my_auto` sets auto top and bottom margins, so a centred column in a scroll viewport keeps its top reachable when it overflows.
* On the web every keyed control with a press handler takes the native mirror button path for focus and keyboard or assistive activation, not only controls marked `native_activation`; pointer presses on the canvas are unchanged. A focused mirror button forwards Tab, Escape, the arrows, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down to the runtime, and a held Enter or Space does not repeat the press.
* A touch holds the focus change its press asked for until the finger lifts, and drops it when the touch turns into a pan, as a browser focuses only on a tap. A scroll step after the press is cancelled skips the press search.
* The web mirror gives each pressable control its ARIA role (checkbox, switch, radio, menu item, tab, option, tree item) and state (pressed, checked, selected, disabled, busy), and `El::busy` marks a control whose action is still running. Mirror attributes are rewritten only when they change.
* `El::unavailable` marks a control that reads as disabled yet keeps focus and its place in the tab order (ARIA `aria-disabled`), in the web mirror and the native tree; the native tree also reports busy.
* Focus groups take `El::focus_axis` and `El::focus_wrap` in place of their role's arrows and wrapping, and Tab returns to the item in a group that last had focus.
* `El::has_popup` names the kind of popup a control opens (ARIA `aria-haspopup`), on the web mirror.
* `El::press_travel` sinks a control while it is pressed and keeps its outer shadows in place, so a key comes down onto its lip.
* The web host tracks effect marks when a compositor is attached, as the native window does, so compositor effect slots draw in the browser.
* `El::caret_block` draws a text field's caret as a block the width of the character after it (a space wide at a line end), as CSS `caret-shape: block`; that character takes the given ink, and a selection or composition hides the block (`tests/caret_block.rs`).
* `El::on_press_down` runs as a primary pointer press lands on an enabled element, before the release activates it, so a key can sound its down-stroke (`tests/press_down.rs`).
* On the web the hidden text field reports the keys it types and every key it releases as physical input, so a focused field's `El::on_physical_input` hears typing as it does on a native host; the password field reports none.
* `El::focus_ring_default` sets the default keyboard focus ring for every control inside an element that sets none of its own, so a theme draws its ring once at its root (`tests/focus_ring_default.rs`). Painting checks an element's own ring before walking up to the focus, so elements without one skip the walk.
* `El::scroll_stop` makes a scroll view a Tab stop while its content overflows and nothing inside it can take focus; focused, the arrow keys scroll it a 40 point line and the page keys a page, and the web mirror shows it as a named region that takes native focus. The web host reconciles its native controls only when the mirror changes, not on every frame.
* `Runtime<S>` is split: `RuntimeCore` holds every field that does not depend on the app's state type and the methods that never touch it (layout, commit, paint, text, scrolling, selection), compiled once; `Runtime<S>` keeps the state, view and handlers, and derefs to the core. A test build with many state types compiled the whole runtime once per type.
* Web mirror elements carry stable ids hashed from their runtime paths, and `El::controls` and `El::active_descendant` reach the mirror as `aria-controls` and `aria-activedescendant` by those ids.
* A mirror sync sends an item that did not change as its place in the last sync (`{"same":n}`); the bridge keeps that element and only checks its order, and asks for a full sync (`a11y_resync`) if it ever lacks one.
* The web mirror shows a `role("listbox")` element as a listbox container around its options, and an element with a control role (option, tab, radio and the like) stays that control without a press handler, so a disabled option still reads as one.
* The workspace's dev and test profiles keep line tables only, not full debug info: a test build of the Rune crate links faster and its target takes 13 GiB instead of 37 GiB.
* `El::layer` makes a non-modal layer (popover, tooltip, list popup): the topmost one, above any modal, hears Escape, a press outside it and its anchor, focus moving out and the window losing focus, each with a `Dismiss` reason, and the app decides (`runtime/dismiss_layer_tests.rs`). A press counts as inside by the point, so text and padding inside a layer are inside.
* A press on a layer's anchor reaches the layer as `Dismiss::AnchorPress` beside the anchor's own handler, so a tooltip closes when its trigger is pressed.
* `El::on_focus_change` tells an element it gained or lost focus and whether the keyboard moved it, so a tooltip opens on keyboard focus and not on a click.
* Finding a node by its path, which each press, hover, dismissal and focus change does, uses the path index and falls back to a scan only for an exiting or unmounted node.
* The web mirror shows `role("tablist")` and a named `role("tabpanel")` as containers. `El::focus_manual` on a focus group lets the arrows move over its radio and tab items without pressing them, for tabs with manual activation.
* The web mirror shows `role("toolbar")` as a named container, and `role("progressbar")` and `role("meter")` as one element each with `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax` and `aria-valuetext` (a progress bar with no value is indeterminate). The mirror's JSON is written straight into one buffer instead of through a `serde_json::Value` tree.
* The items an arrow key moves between come from the group's own subtree, with the membership test before the reachability one, instead of every node on the page.
* On start the web host corrects the canvas height as well as its width when Chromium's emulated device scale reports CSS pixels, so the chat no longer lays out at half height and scrolls its content under the tab bar.
* `text::add_fonts` registers fallback fonts on a running app: every text system on the thread (windows, overlays, the measurer) registers them as script and CJK fallbacks on its next frame and lays out again, and `font_epoch` moves.
* Web input stops untrusted (`isTrusted` false) input types in the window capture phase, before the page's listeners and winit's. Mirror presses and focus name the browser's trust and the mirror revision they were rendered from, and the runtime refuses any other (`runtime/input/provenance.rs`).
* The `examples` directory and its `[[example]]` entries are not vendored; metldr builds none of them.
